lesson.title: range(): Generating Number Sequences on Demand
lesson.summary: The range() function produces a sequence of integers from a start, stop, and step you specify, and it is the most common way to control exactly how many times a for loop runs.
lesson.body:
When a for loop needs to repeat a specific number of times rather than walk over an existing list, Python's built-in range() function is almost always the tool for the job. Calling range() produces a sequence of evenly spaced integers, generated on demand rather than stored all at once in memory, which makes it efficient even for enormous counts like a million repetitions. A for loop can iterate directly over that sequence just as naturally as it would over an actual list.

range() accepts one, two, or three arguments, and each form is genuinely useful. With a single argument, range(stop) produces integers starting at 0 up to, but not including, stop. With two arguments, range(start, stop) begins counting at start instead of always starting at 0. With three arguments, range(start, stop, step) counts by step instead of by 1, and step can even be negative to count downward toward a smaller stop value. The single most common beginner mistake is forgetting that stop is always exclusive: range(5) produces 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, never a 5, which trips up plenty of programs that expect one more value than they actually get.

Here is a three-argument example:
for i in range(2, 10, 2):
    print(i)
Trace it precisely. i starts at 2, which is less than 10, so 2 is printed. Then i becomes 4, still less than 10, and it is printed. Then 6 is printed, then 8 is printed. Then i would become 10, but 10 is not less than 10, so the loop stops right there without printing it. The full output is 2, 4, 6, 8, each on its own line; ten itself is never reached because the stop value is exclusive by design.

The single-argument form is the one you will reach for constantly, especially for the "do this N times" pattern, where the actual counter value does not even matter to the logic inside the loop:
for _ in range(5):
    print("Hello!")
This prints "Hello!" exactly five times, using range(5) purely to control the repeat count, with the underscore signaling to readers that the loop variable itself is never actually used inside the body. range() is also frequently paired with len() to loop over the valid indices of a list, as in range(len(my_list)), whenever a task needs the position of each item rather than, or in addition to, the item's value itself.

It is worth remembering that range() does not build and store a full list of numbers in memory the way typing out [2, 4, 6, 8] would. It produces values lazily, one at a time, as the loop asks for the next one, which is why range(1000000) is created instantly and costs almost no memory, even though looping over it still takes real time to run to completion.

Because range() is almost always the iterable a for loop draws from when you're not already iterating over an existing collection, it is worth thinking of range() and the for loop as a matched pair: the for loop supplies the repeating structure, and range() supplies the specific, precisely controlled sequence of numbers to repeat over.
